 What to Know On Election Day 
 From state supreme court races to constitutional amendments, from court disputes over polling hours to laws mandating certification, here’s what voters should understand for going to the polls and what happens after.
 By 
 Alicia Bannon
 Published: November 2, 2026

 You’re reading  State Court Report’s  biweekly newsletter.   Subscribe to receive it in your inbox . 
 On Tuesday, voters across the United States will cast their ballots. Here are some of the key things to know for Election Day, along with State Court Report articles that offer the bigger picture.
 Twenty-three states will be holding elections for 42 state supreme court seats. With so many high-profile congressional and gubernatorial races this year, state supreme court elections have largely stayed under the radar even as they have the potential to shape the legal landscape in states across the country. State Court Report founding editor Douglas Keith’s election preview highlights some of the big ones to watch tomorrow. 
 In Montana, district judges Amy Eddy and Dan Wilson are facing off in a nonpartisan election in which Eddy has attracted support from liberal groups and Wilson describes himself as a “judicial conservative.” Montana’s state high court has taken an active role in enforcing state constitutional rights in recent years, including protecting the rights of transgender people and striking down restrictive voting laws, and has often divided on 5–2 or 4–3 lines. Tomorrow’s election doesn’t present an opportunity to change the court’s majority, but it will affect how closely divided the court is in 2028, when two seats currently held by left-leaning justices will be up for election. Likely for this reason, the Montana Supreme Court election has attracted nearly $3 million in spending.
 Similar dynamics are at play in North Carolina, where Justice Anita Earls, a Democrat and former civil rights lawyer, is running against challenger Sarah Stevens, a former Republican state legislator, in a partisan election. Conservative justices on North Carolina’s high court currently enjoy a 5–2 majority, and three seats now held by Republicans will be up for election in 2028. Like Montana, North Carolina’s 2028 election is likely to be a major fight over the court’s future direction; this year’s precursor has attracted more than $8 million in spending. Other states with judicial elections to watch tomorrow include Michigan, Missouri, Ohio, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming.
 Despite plenty of noise, states have clear processes for resolving certification questions and other election disputes. There are also significant legal issues to watch tomorrow and in the days and weeks that follow. Attorney General Todd Blanche has stated that the Department of Justice may seek to block states from certifying certain election results, and the DOJ recently filed a federal lawsuit asserting that it may seek to do so in Alaska’s U.S. Senate race. In recent years, rogue local officials in some states have also refused to certify valid elections based on election denialism theories. While these efforts can generate confusion and even fear, the good news is that the law around election certification is very clear: Election officials don’t have the authority to conduct freewheeling investigations or to refuse to certify final election results, and the federal government simply doesn’t play a role in the certification process. The Brennan Center’s Lauren Miller Karalunas offers an in-depth overview of how election certification works, plus a detailed breakdown of the processes in key battleground states.
 Another legal issue to watch is the potential for ballot seizures. In recent months, search warrants related to recent elections have been issued by both federal and state judges. Former Ohio Chief Justice Maureen O’Connor and the Brennan Center’s Hayne Yoon discuss considerations for judges in evaluating election-related search warrant applications, including how judges can institute procedures to safeguard election records. And the State Democracy Research Initiative’s Derek Clinger analyzes two recent California Supreme Court rulings on this issue and the lessons they offer to other states. 
 Finally, it’s worth noting that no matter how much election administrators do to prepare in advance, something is going to go wrong somewhere. Unanticipated circumstances can lead to requests to extend poll hours. State Court Report provides a great overview by a former election administrator about the rules courts apply when considering these requests.
 Constitutional change is on the ballot. One of the most substantial ways that state constitutions differ from the U.S. Constitution is the ease with which they can be amended. Between 2005 and 2025, states across the country ratified more than a thousand constitutional amendments, many of which established new constitutional rights, according to an analysis by Howard University political scientist Robinson Woodward-Burns. Seventeen states currently provide for a citizen-initiative process for amending state constitutions, and in every state but Delaware, proposed amendments must be ratified by voters. 
 This year, a number of significant proposed amendments and other measures are on the ballot, as State Court Report ’s Erin Geiger Smith explains . Measures that would both expand and restrict rights are up before voters in areas including voting, redistricting, reproductive rights, LGBTQ+ rights, and more.
 Alicia Bannon is editor in chief for  State Court Report . She is also director of the Judiciary Program at the Brennan Center for Justice.
